title: Episode 16: The Black Bean Lottery of 1843: Texas Soldiers and the Jar of Death
description:
In 1843, following the ill-fated Mier Expedition into Mexico, 176 Texian soldiers were captured and marched toward Mexico City. Mexican dictator Santa Anna ordered every tenth man executed. The condemned were chosen through the infamous Black Bean Lottery: an earthen clay jar containing 159 white beans and 17 black beans.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the turbulent decade of the Republic of Texas, border warfare with Mexico was marked by bitter skirmishes, legendary bravery, and terrifying cruelty. Nowhere was that friction more harrowing than in the spring of eighteen forty-three, in the remote northern deserts of Mexico. Following a rogue military raid across the Rio Grande known as the Mier Expedition, nearly two hundred Texian fighters surrendered after running out of ammunition. Enraged by their defiance, Mexican dictator Antonio López de Santa Anna issued a brutal executive decree: every tenth man was to be shot by a firing squad. To select the condemned, Mexican officers blindfolded the prisoners and ordered them to reach into an earthen clay jar filled with beans. A white bean meant life and prison; a black bean meant execution at sunrise. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE ROGUE MARCH ACROSS THE RIO GRANDE
In late eighteen forty-two, the young Republic of Texas was on high military alert. Six years had passed since General Sam Houston defeated Antonio López de Santa Anna at San Jacinto, winning Texian independence. Yet Mexico refused to recognize the treaties, launching sudden cavalry raids across the Rio Grande that captured San Antonio twice in a single year. In response, Texas President Sam Houston authorized General Alexander Somervell to lead seven hundred volunteers to patrol the border and deter further Mexican incursions. When Somervell determined that an invasion of Mexico was militarily reckless and ordered his men to disband and return home, over three hundred hotheaded frontiersmen mutinied. Led by Captain William S. Fisher and fiery ranger Ewen Cameron, these men refused to retreat, voting to cross the Rio Grande and assault the Mexican border city of Ciudad Mier to seize supplies and horses. On Christmas Day, eighteen forty-two, the Texian raiders attacked Mier in the freezing winter rain, engaging over two thousand Mexican regular infantrymen and cavalry commanded by General Pedro de Ampudia. For twenty-four hours, the Texians fought from house to house with deadly rifle accuracy, inflicting hundreds of casualties. However, cut off from their supply lines, low on water, and completely out of gunpowder, Captain Fisher agreed to an honorable surrender, with General Ampudia promising in writing that the Texians would be treated as prisoners of war. The Texian volunteers were armed with Kentucky long rifles and revolving pistols, possessing lethal marksmanship but carrying only forty rounds of ammunition per man.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE ESCAPE AT SALADO
The promise of honorable treatment proved to be completely hollow. Instead of being paroled, the two hundred and sixty Texian prisoners were bound in heavy iron shackles and marched on foot deep into the interior of Mexico toward the dungeons of Perote Castle. As the column marched under brutal sun through the desert near the hacienda of Salado in Coahuila, the Texians realized that their ultimate fate was likely execution or permanent forced labor in Mexican silver mines. Led by the towering Scottish-born ranger Captain Ewen Cameron, the prisoners organized a daring, desperate escape. On the morning of February eleventh, eighteen forty-three, as the morning cavalry patrol changed guard, Cameron shouted the secret signal: 'Now, boys, go for them!' Unarmed, the Texians charged the Mexican guards, wrestling carbines and sabers from their hands in hand-to-hand combat. They overwhelmed the garrison, captured two hundred horses, and broke out into the vast Chihuahuan desert. However, in their desperation to evade pursuing cavalry, the Texians made a fatal navigational error: fearing the main road, they abandoned their horses and plunged into the trackless, waterless mountains of the Sierra Madre. Within days, under the scorching desert sun, water ran out. Men were reduced to eating snakes, cactus roots, and finally drinking their own horses' blood. Delirious, barefoot, and dying of dehydration, one hundred and seventy-six exhausted survivors collapsed and were recaptured by Mexican cavalry. Cameron was a legendary Scottish-born frontiersman who had survived countless Indian skirmishes, earning a reputation among both Texians and Mexicans as a warrior of superhuman endurance.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: SANTA ANNA'S ORDER OF DECIMATION
When news of the violent breakout reached Mexico City, General Antonio López de Santa Anna flew into a volcanic rage. The dictator viewed the Texians not as legitimate soldiers of a sovereign republic, but as armed filibusters and treasonous pirates who deserved no mercy. Santa Anna immediately signed a secret executive order commanding that every single recaptured Texian soldier be stood against an adobe wall and shot dead on the spot. However, the governor of Coahuila, Francisco Mexía, and senior field commander General José María Mexía were horrified by the order, flatly refusing to carry out an outright mass slaughter of surrendered prisoners of war. Foreign diplomats from Great Britain and the United States also intervened, warning Santa Anna that murdering all one hundred and seventy-six men would trigger an international diplomatic crisis and likely provoke an American military invasion. Furious at having his absolute authority challenged, Santa Anna grudgingly compromised. He invoked the ancient, brutal Roman military practice of decimation: instead of executing the entire company, every tenth man would be put to death. Seventeen Texians would die, and their identities would be determined through the pure, horrifying chance of a lottery. Mexican field officers openly voiced their moral disgust with the execution order, warning that executing captured soldiers violated the customs of civilized nations.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE EARTHEN JAR AND THE BLACK BEANS
On the afternoon of March twenty-fifth, eighteen forty-three, the recaptured prisoners were lined up in the central courtyard of the Hacienda Salado under heavy armed guard. A Mexican colonel named Domingo Huerta placed an earthen clay jar on a wooden bench in the center of the yard. Inside the jar, Huerta dropped precisely one hundred and seventy-six dried beans: one hundred and fifty-nine white beans, and exactly seventeen black beans. The beans were identical in size and shape, mixed thoroughly, and covered with a thick silk handkerchief to prevent anyone from seeing inside. Huerta announced the rules through a translator: each man would step forward in alphabetical order, reach his bare hand into the jar, and pull out a single bean. A white bean meant life, chains, and the march to Perote Prison. A black bean meant immediate death by firing squad at sunset. The scene was agonizingly tense. The prisoners were emaciated, filthy, and covered in desert dust, yet they faced the jar with extraordinary frontier defiance. To ensure fairness, Captain Ewen Cameron was ordered to draw first. Cameron stepped forward with steady hands, reached into the jar, and withdrew a white bean, shouting to his men: 'Well, boys, I'm safe!' However, Mexican officers had deliberately placed the seventeen black beans near the top of the jar, so the officers who drew early faced catastrophic odds. Father Ramón, a local Catholic priest from the nearby mission, walked among the prisoners, offering the last rites of the church and praying for the souls of whoever would draw the fatal black beans.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SEVENTEEN CONDEMNED
One by one, the Texian prisoners stepped forward to draw their fate from the jar. Men displayed astonishing courage. When Captain William Eastland drew a black bean, he held it up to the afternoon sun, smiled wryly, and remarked that he had always been unlucky in lotteries. A seventeen-year-old boy named Robert Beard was trembling in terror, but his older friend stepped forward to comfort him. Major Robert Dunham, a pious young man from Tennessee, asked the Mexican officers for a pencil and paper, writing a farewell letter to his mother in which he stated that he faced death without fear and forgave his captors. By four o'clock in the afternoon, all seventeen black beans had been drawn. The seventeen condemned Texians were immediately separated from their comrades, placed in heavy leg irons, and moved into a small adobe room on the southern side of the courtyard. The survivors who had drawn white beans wept openly, embracing their condemned friends through the barred windows, sharing their last tobacco scraps and prayers. The seventeen men requested that they be shot in the front rather than the back, so they could face their executioners like soldiers. At dusk, Mexican infantry formed firing squads behind the adobe walls. Volleys of musketry echoed through the desert canyon, extinguishing seventeen Texian lives in the twilight. As each shot echoed through the courtyard, the surviving Texians knelt in prayer, holding each other's hands and reciting the twenty-third psalm in the fading daylight.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE MARCH TO PEROTE AND THE LEGEND
The surviving Texians were forced to resume their grueling march across Mexico, ultimately reaching the colossal fortress of Castle Perote in Veracruz. Even there, Santa Anna was not finished with his vengeance. Furious that the defiant Scottish captain Ewen Cameron had survived the lottery, Santa Anna issued a special order for Cameron to be executed by a separate firing squad while imprisoned at Huehuetoca. Cameron stood before the rifles, refused a blindfold, bared his chest, and gave the command to fire himself. Over the next two years, international diplomatic pressure mounted from Washington and London. In September of eighteen forty-four, Santa Anna finally released the surviving Texian prisoners, who returned home to Texas as celebrated martyrs. The Black Bean Lottery became an indelible part of the Texas founding legend, immortalized in paintings, songs, and historical memorials across the state. In eighteen forty-eight, after the Mexican-American War, the bones of the seventeen men executed at Salado were exhumed by Texas Rangers, returned to Texas with full military honors, and buried in a massive stone tomb on Monument Hill in La Grange, overlooking the Colorado River. The story of the earthen jar and the black beans remains an enduring testament to the grit, brotherhood, and unflinching frontier courage of those who dared carve a nation out of the wilderness. Today, Monument Hill State Historic Site preserves the stone tomb containing the remains of the seventeen heroes of the Black Bean Lottery, overlooking the rolling hills of Central Texas.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Black Bean Lottery of 1843 stands as one of the most chilling, cinematic moments of frontier history. It reminds us that the line between life and death on the frontier often came down to the luck of the draw, and that true courage is not the absence of fear, but facing the earthen jar with an unyielding heart. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next time for another forgotten chapter of history. Until then, stay curious.
